name: Erik Hartman
description: Erik Hartman is a computational biologist at Lund University and a visiting research scholar at Penn, studying encrypted peptides and computational protein and peptide design.
introduction: I study how proteins give rise to bioactive peptides, build computational methods to discover and design them, and model molecular changes during infection.
focus: I’m interested in how mathematics and machine learning can help us understand biology, from interpreting molecular data to designing proteins and peptides. I am particularly interested in fragments of proteins that have biological functions of their own, so-called encrypted peptides. I study how these fragments are generated and what roles they may play across the tree of life.

research.title: Encrypted peptides
research.description: I investigate bioactive peptides released through protein degradation, particularly antimicrobial peptides and their role in host defense.

figure.alt: A folded protein made of blue-gray ribbons contains a coral peptide segment, shown separately after release.
figure.caption: Discovering bioactive fragments hidden within proteins.

research.title: Protein and peptide design
research.description: I develop methods for protein and peptide design using machine learning, Bayesian optimization, and biological information.

figure.alt: Four structure-informed protein and peptide folds lead through a sequence-refinement cycle to a coral peptide helix in a blue-gray protein cleft.
figure.caption: Learning from candidate sequences to guide molecular design.

research.title: Infectious disease modelling
research.description: I use proteomics and machine learning to study molecular changes during infection and model how disease progresses over time.

figure.alt: Host molecular measurements feeding into branching disease trajectories, with one path highlighted in coral.
figure.caption: Connecting molecular measurements with disease trajectories.
